I could feel engaged, like I was connected to people and doing something that mattered. Yes… I think that’s closer to what finally made me feel like I should come in, honestly. I don’t know if I can map it perfectly onto a clean two-week block, but there have definitely been stretches where the part of me that used to reach for things has just gone very quiet.

So yes, I’d say there have been periods where I had very little interest or pleasure nearly every day, even if I’m hesitant about the exact timing.

I used to really take pleasure in my work, and yoga, and going to galleries, even journaling — those were things that helped me feel connected to myself. And lately it’s like I can’t quite access that. I’m doing the motions, but there’s not much there behind it. That’s what scared me enough to make the appointment.\n\nDoctor: Did this start after a specific stressful event or major life change?\n\nPatient: Yes… I think there was a point where it started, or at least where I can trace it back to. It’s been about eight months now, maybe a little over, since we took my older relative into our apartment. That was the big change.\n\nI don’t know if I noticed it immediately in a clean way, like “oh, this is when everything changed,” but looking back, that’s when this whole shift in how I’m thinking and working and connecting with people really began. It’s like my mind got more crowded, and at the same time I started feeling more distant from people and from the things I usually relied on. At first I told myself it was just the adjustment, because having another person in the apartment changes the whole rhythm of the place, and I thought I’d adapt. But it’s been months now, and it hasn’t really gone back to normal.\n\nDoctor: Over the past couple of weeks, have you been feeling down or depressed most days?\n\nPatient: I’m not sure I would call it “depressed,” exactly. That word feels a little too simple for what it’s been like. Over the past couple of weeks, I’ve had days where I feel flat or sort of muted, like things don’t really land emotionally the way they used to. But if you mean sad all day, crying, that kind of obvious heaviness… no, not most days in that clear way.\n\nIt’s more that I wake up and there’s this sense of effort around everything, and I keep wondering if I’m just tired or overwhelmed. I can still get through the day, and sometimes I can seem fine from the outside, so it’s hard for me to know how to answer. I wouldn’t say I’ve felt happy, exactly, but “down most days”... maybe somewhat, but not in a way I can neatly label.\n\nDoctor: Over the past two weeks, have you lost interest or pleasure in things you usually enjoy?\n\nPatient: Yes… I think that’s probably the biggest part of it, honestly. It’s not that I never do those things anymore, but the feeling I used to get from them is just… much quieter, almost absent sometimes.\n\nWork used to give me a real sense of meaning, even on hard days. I could feel engaged, like I was connected to people and doing something that mattered. Now I still show up, I still go through what I’m supposed to do, but it feels more like I’m completing tasks than actually being there in the way I used to be.\n\nAnd outside of work, it’s similar. Yoga used to help me feel grounded, galleries used to make me curious, journaling used to feel like I was sorting myself out. Lately I either don’t reach for those things, or if I do, I’m kind of just… performing the habit. Like I know they’re things I used to enjoy, so I try them, but I don’t get much pleasure from them. Even with people, I don’t naturally reach out the way I used to. I’m mostly just moving through obligations.\n\nDoctor: Have you been worrying a lot more than usual lately?\n\nPatient: I don’t know if I’d say “worrying a lot more,” exactly. I mean, I do think about things a lot, and I can get stuck turning things over in my head, but I’m not sure it feels like ordinary worry in the way I would usually describe it.\n\nWhen I think of worrying, I think of being anxious about bills, or someone’s health, or whether I made a mistake at work, that kind of thing. This feels harder to categorize. Some days I’m preoccupied, definitely, and I can spend too much time trying to make sense of things or replaying conversations or wondering what I’m missing. But I don’t know that I’ve noticed a clear increase in worry, like constant anxious fear.\n\nSo… maybe some, but I’m not sure. I wouldn’t want to overstate it.\n\nDoctor: Have these changes started to interfere with how well you function in daily life?\n\nPatient: Yes… though I’ve been trying not to admit that, I think. I’m still showing up to work, so part of me wants to say I’m functioning, because I’m not, you know, staying home or completely falling apart. I get dressed, I go in, I see people, I answer emails. From the outside it probably looks like I’m basically doing my job.\n\nBut I’m definitely not functioning at my usual level. I’ve missed some grant deadlines, which is really unlike me. That’s the kind of thing I normally keep track of almost automatically, or at least I used to. And my supervisor hasn’t made a big dramatic issue of it, but I’ve noticed she’s quietly moved some of my more demanding clients to other clinicians. She framed it very gently, like redistributing caseloads, but I know what it means. Or at least I think I do. It’s because I’m not as sharp or as present as I usually am.\n\nSo yes, it is interfering. Not in a catastrophic way, maybe, but enough that other people are adjusting around me, and that feels… embarrassing. I mean, I don’t want to make it sound like I’m blaming them, because that feels awful and unfair, and it’s more complicated than that. But the timing is pretty clear to me.\n\nThis whole change in how I’m thinking, and how I’m working, and how connected I feel with people has been going on for about eight months, which is basically since we took my older relative into our apartment. At first I thought it was just an adjustment period, you know, everyone needing to get used to the new routines and less space and the emotional weight of it. I kept telling myself it would settle.\n\nBut it hasn’t really gone back to normal. It feels like that was the point where things shifted, and I’ve been kind of moving through life differently since then. So yes, I do think it’s mainly connected to that, or at least it started around then.\n\nDoctor: For most of the last eight months, have you felt sad or down nearly every day?\n\nPatient: I don’t think so… not nearly every day, no. I mean, I’ve had days where I feel heavy or discouraged, especially when I’m aware that I’m not keeping up the way I usually do, and that can feel pretty awful. But I wouldn’t describe the last eight months as me being sad or down most days.\n\nIt’s more like… I get tired of myself, or frustrated, or unsettled. There are moments where I feel low, definitely, but then other days I’m just trying to get through things and I’m not necessarily sad. So if you mean a persistent depressed mood almost every day, I don’t think that fits exactly.\n\nDoctor: Over the past six months, have you felt anxious or on edge more days than not?\n\nPatient: I’m not sure I’d describe it that way exactly. I mean, I’ve definitely felt tense at times, and there are days when I feel sort of wound up or watchful, like I’m waiting for something to go wrong. But “more days than not” over six months… I don’t know. That feels hard to say.\n\nI think I’d have to really look back and count it, because some weeks feel worse than others, and then other times I’m just distracted or tired or preoccupied, not necessarily anxious. So I wouldn’t want to say yes too strongly if you mean a steady, almost constant anxiety. I’ve noticed stress, definitely, but I’m not sure it’s been that frequent in the way you’re asking.\n\nDoctor: Does having your older relative living with you still feel like an ongoing source of stress for you?\n\nPatient: I guess… yes, in some ways it still does, but I’m not sure I can separate out how much of the stress is specifically from them living with us versus everything that comes with that arrangement, if that makes sense.\n\nIt’s not like every single moment is stressful, and I don’t want to make them sound like the problem. They’re family, and I care about them. But having another person in the home, especially an older relative who needs consideration and has their own routines and needs, changes the whole feeling of the apartment. There’s less privacy, less quiet, less of that feeling that I can fully decompress when I get home.\n\nSo yes, I’d say it still feels like an ongoing pressure. Maybe not a crisis every day, but a kind of background strain that hasn’t really gone away.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel emotionally drained or burned out by the ongoing demands at home?\n\nPatient: I’m not completely sure how to answer that. “Burned out” feels like a strong word, and I don’t know if I’d say that exactly. I do feel tired by it sometimes, emotionally tired, like there’s always one more thing to think about at home and I can’t quite fully relax.\n\nBut then part of me thinks, well, that’s just what family situations are like, and maybe I’m making too much of it. It’s not like I’m constantly at the end of my rope. Some days I handle it fine, or I just go through the motions and don’t think about it too much.\n\nSo… drained at times, yes, probably. It’s more like this ongoing background fatigue from having to stay considerate and aware of everyone in the house.\n\nDoctor: During this past eight months, was there ever a period of two weeks in a row when you felt down or depressed most of the day nearly every day?\n\nPatient: I don’t know if I can say that clearly. I don’t want to overstate it. I wouldn’t say I’ve felt happy, exactly, but “down most days”... maybe somewhat, but not in a way I can neatly label.\n\nDoctor: Over the past two weeks, have you lost interest or pleasure in things you usually enjoy?\n\nPatient: Yes… I think that’s probably the biggest part of it, honestly. It’s not that I never do those things anymore, but the feeling I used to get from them is just… much quieter, almost absent sometimes.\n\nWork used to give me a real sense of meaning, even on hard days. I could feel engaged, like I was connected to people and doing something that mattered. Now I still show up, I still go through what I’m supposed to do, but it feels more like I’m completing tasks than actually being there in the way I used to be.\n\nAnd outside of work, it’s similar. Yoga used to help me feel grounded, galleries used to make me curious, journaling used to feel like I was sorting myself out. Lately I either don’t reach for those things, or if I do, I’m kind of just… performing the habit. Like I know they’re things I used to enjoy, so I try them, but I don’t get much pleasure from them. Even with people, I don’t naturally reach out the way I used to. I’m mostly just moving through obligations.\n\nDoctor: Have you been worrying a lot more than usual lately?\n\nPatient: I don’t know if I’d say “worrying a lot more,” exactly. I mean, I do think about things a lot, and I can get stuck turning things over in my head, but I’m not sure it feels like ordinary worry in the way I would usually describe it.\n\nWhen I think of worrying, I think of being anxious about bills, or someone’s health, or whether I made a mistake at work, that kind of thing. This feels harder to categorize. Some days I’m preoccupied, definitely, and I can spend too much time trying to make sense of things or replaying conversations or wondering what I’m missing. But I don’t know that I’ve noticed a clear increase in worry, like constant anxious fear.\n\nSo… maybe some, but I’m not sure. I wouldn’t want to overstate it.\n\nDoctor: Have these changes started to interfere with how well you function in daily life?\n\nPatient: Yes… though I’ve been trying not to admit that, I think. I’m still showing up to work, so part of me wants to say I’m functioning, because I’m not, you know, staying home or completely falling apart. I get dressed, I go in, I see people, I answer emails.
